title: Labor ‘knew of negative equity risks in 5pc plan’
full_text:
Treasury officials were told Anthony Albanese’s 5 per cent home deposit scheme could lead to first-home buyers being more vulnerable to high loan-to-value ratios, according to internal department documents revealing conflicting views on negative equity impacts.
Amid concerns first-home buyers accessing the government’s expanded and generous home deposit scheme will be caught out by plunging house prices, newly released Treasury documents reveal that officials accepted negative equity could be a problem for some borrowers.
In an e-mail between senior Treasury bureaucrats on April 9, a leading official discussed a conversation with veteran economist Saul Eslake, who raised the point that “the share of bank lending to first-home buyers has increasingly gone to those with high loan-to-value ratios”.
The revelation comes as auction clearance rates pushed above 50 per cent but still stayed below historic levels for the 11th week in a row since Labor announced housing tax changes in the budget. Property data firm Cotality attributed this to a low withdrawal rate – the rate at which properties are pulled from the market before the auction – and a low share of properties going up for auction.
The 5 per cent deposit scheme discussed in the Treasury documents allows eligible first-home buyers to take out loans on a 5 per cent deposit, without having to pay for lenders mortgage insurance.
“Saul’s observation that lending at high loan-to-value (LVR) ratios has increased is correct, but we note that this was the expected policy outcome. Generally speaking, highly leveraged borrowers are more vulnerable to financial pressures if interest rates rise. They tend to have smaller financial buffers than other groups and are more likely to fall into negative equity,” Treasury documents said. “It is important to note, however, that loan applications must be assessed with a serviceability buffer, which is 3 per cent in the case of first-home buyers who took up the 5 per cent deposit scheme.
“APRA and the RBA generally view that risks to the financial system from those who participate in the 5 per cent deposit scheme are limited, despite their high LVRs. This is because the government guarantees up to 15 per cent of the property value in case of default.”
Mr Eslake said he was not officially engaged by Treasury for any advice and he instead talks to Treasury officials “from time to time”.
Treasury, in response to a Freedom of Information request, identified 26 documents related to the impact of the government’s 5 per cent deposit scheme on the prudential assessment of high loan-to-value ratio lending risk. Of those documents – including ministerial briefs, talking points, estimates briefings and agency updates – 17 were released in full, five were partially released and four documents were refused because of impacts on “foreign relations” and exemptions related to cabinet and other provisions.
The FOI, lodged by opposition housing and homelessness spokesman Andrew Bragg on June 1, requested access to all correspondence, emails and communications “in relation to the impact of the government’s 5 per cent deposits scheme on the prudential assessment of high loan-to-value ratio lending risk”.
The Australian last week revealed people who own property overseas are still eligible for Labor’s expanded deposit scheme despite it being aimed at first-home buyers. It was also revealed that taxpayers were underwriting first-home buyer couples making up to $675,000 a year amid warnings that the lack of means-testing was warping an already troubled property market for both buyers and renters. Some economists have described the more generous scheme as “middle class welfare”.
Ahead of the Reserve Bank board meeting on Tuesday, Senator Bragg said the Albanese government had “turned a targeted scheme into an uncapped free-for-all, removing income caps and limits on places”.
“This was vote-buying, pure and simple. Treasury admitted internally that the 5 per cent deposit scheme led to more risky loans and a surge in high loan-to-value lending. These are the very same loans that are most exposed when prices fall because buyers have smaller buffers and are more likely to end up in negative equity,” Senator Bragg told The Australian.
“The documents show that the economist Saul Eslake raised the alarm about the growing share of first-home buyers taking out high-LVR loans. Treasury’s own response accepted that highly leveraged borrowers are more vulnerable and more likely to fall into negative equity.”
According to documents released by Treasury, Senator Bragg was mentioned by officials in briefing notes 21 times.
Senator Bragg said the RBA had been “more upfront about the upward impacts of the scheme on housing demand, prices, and high leverage rates/negative equity”.
In a previous response to Senator Bragg, the RBA agreed with Cotality that “the step-up in growth rates coincides with the 5 per cent deposit scheme going live in October … This will likely add to housing demand, especially around lower-to-middle price points of the market”.
Senator Bragg expressed concern that Australians accessing Labor’s scheme would be “living through the nightmare of negative equity”.
“All Australians are living through the recklessness of 5 per cent deposits through its inflating of prices at the entry level. This is most pronounced because of Labor’s housing supply failure and simultaneous migration bonanza. The 5 per cent fiasco is bigger than Labor’s routine housing incompetence. Labor is getting the public service to run cover for their political disasters like its 5 per cent mortgage free-for-all,” he said.
“In summary, Labor has wasted billions on housing for 30,000 fewer houses a year. Australia needs a government with housing policies that actually create new supply. That is the only way to solve the housing crisis.”
Contacted for comment, Housing Minister Clare O’Neil’s office noted that Senator Bragg had previously said entry-level house prices were too expensive and “must come down”.
“The 5 per cent deposit scheme remains robust with a less than 0.01 per cent default rate, and no amount of confected Liberal outrage will change the fact that Labor has helped more than 260,000 Australians into homeownership through the scheme,” a spokesman for Ms O’Neil said.
“Under the Coalition in 2019, the rate of negative equity was more than double what it is now and yet it didn’t rate a single parliamentary mention from them.
“Labor’s making headway with repairing a broken housing system that locks out first-home buyers by implementing systemic reforms that improve supply, and levelling the playing field for Australians looking to get into their first home.”
